title: How to brief a small-business website for 2027
description: A practical brief template for owners planning a 2027 website: priority customer action, service hierarchy, assets, integrations, editing ownership, budget and sign-off, plus a completed electrician example.
summary: A useful small-business website brief names the priority customer action, ranks the services worth selling, lists real pages and assets, states integrations and editing responsibility, and sets budget and sign-off expectations. It gives a designer enough context to quote accurately instead of guessing at scope, platform and content.
takeaways: Brief the job you want the site to do first: the customer action, the service priority and the success measure.
Give the designer real assets, existing URLs, integrations and the name of the person who will edit the site.
Use the electrician sample brief as a worksheet, then send it to a shortlist so quotes are comparable.

sections.title: A brief is a buying decision, not a wish list
sections.body:
A useful small-business website brief does not try to sound impressive. It tells the person pricing the job what the site has to accomplish, what already exists, what systems it must talk to and who will be responsible for changing it later. That is the difference between a quote built on facts and a quote padded with assumptions.

When I ask an owner for a brief, I am really asking for a set of decisions. If those decisions are still floating around inside the company, the designer has to guess. Guessing is expensive. It shows up later as extra pages, unclear copy, missing photography, platform arguments and a launch that keeps moving.

For most Okanagan service businesses, the right brief is short enough to complete in a working session or two, but specific enough that two different designers would understand the same project. If you want help with that kind of planning, start with my web design work rather than with a template alone.

sections.title: Start with the customer action you want
sections.body:
The first thing to write down is the main action you want a visitor to take. For one business that might be a phone call. For another it might be a quote request, a booked estimate, a showroom visit or an email asking for availability. If everything is important, the website will feel like a brochure with too many doors.

Then write the second and third actions. A good site can support more than one outcome, but the hierarchy matters. The homepage, the main navigation and the strongest calls to action should usually serve the first choice. Secondary actions can live in the right places without competing for the same attention.

It also helps to name what you do not want the site to do. Suppose an owner knows that online payment would create administrative problems, or that a complex configurator would produce bad requests. Saying that early is useful. It prevents the design conversation from drifting toward features that look exciting in a portfolio and create work in the business.

sections.title: Rank the services before you design the pages
sections.body:
Small businesses often offer more than their websites explain well. A landscaping company may also handle snow removal. An electrician may do service calls, renovation work and a smaller amount of commercial maintenance. A studio may sell strategy, design and ongoing support. The brief should say which of those deserves the most space and the clearest path to enquiry.

This is not only a sitemap question. It affects photography, proof, page length, calls to action and search structure. Google's own SEO starter guide still points back to making pages easy for people and search engines to understand. If your best service is buried under three pages of generalities, both have to work harder than they should.

A practical way to do this is to sort services into three groups: the work you want more of, the work you will keep because it is profitable or steady, and the work you mention only to avoid confusion. That gives the designer a clear instruction about emphasis instead of a demand that everything be featured equally.

sections.title: List the real assets and the pages you already have
sections.body:
Before asking for a new look, gather what is actually usable. That includes the logo files, brand colours, fonts if you have them, photography, video, diagrams, downloadable documents, staff bios, service descriptions and any copy that still sounds like the business. It also includes the existing website itself. Old pages often contain service details, location language and customer questions that should not be thrown out without review.

Make a simple inventory with three columns: keep, improve and remove. A page may have the wrong design but the right explanation. A photo may be unusable while the testimonial beside it is still strong. An old PDF may be ugly and still be the only place a technical specification is written clearly.

This is also the moment to collect examples of sites you like, but be specific about why. "I like the clean look" is weak. "I like how this page separates emergency repair from planned installation" is useful. Good reference points help a designer understand taste, while vague mood boards usually produce a prettier version of the same problem.

sections.title: Name the integrations and the editing owner
sections.body:
Websites rarely sit alone for long. Your brief should say whether enquiries need to go into a CRM, whether email signups must sync with a newsletter platform, whether bookings need to connect to a calendar and whether analytics or call tracking are already in use. If you do not know, say that too. "We think our form entries go somewhere" is still a useful fact if it is written honestly.

Just as important is the editing owner. Who will update services, add photos, post news, change staff profiles or review enquiries? One person should be named, even if several people will help. Without that, the site is designed around an imaginary team and then handed to a business that does not have the time, skill or interest to maintain it.

These details shape platform and build decisions. They also prevent a common small-business problem: a beautiful site that depends on a workflow nobody asked for. The best choice for one owner can be the wrong choice for another, even when both need a professional-looking website.

sections.title: Put budget assumptions and sign-off in writing
sections.body:
A brief does not need to publish your maximum budget, but it should explain the assumptions behind the project. Are you expecting a compact brochure site, a rebuild of an existing structure, custom copywriting, new photography, search work, hosting changes or ongoing support? If those items are left vague, every quote becomes hard to compare.

I also like to see the approval path named. Who signs off on the sitemap, the design, the copy and the final launch? If the owner approves strategy but a manager approves page copy, say so. If a committee has to review the website, agree who consolidates its feedback and who makes the final decision before production begins.

This is where owners can save themselves real frustration. A clear brief makes it much easier to compare website quotes because each designer is responding to the same scope. If cost is still the open question, it also helps to understand the broader Okanagan website cost picture before asking for fixed numbers.

sections.title: A sample brief for an electrician
sections.body:
Suppose a hypothetical Okanagan electrician wants a new website for 2027. The owner is busy, the current site is old, and the business gets a mix of emergency calls, renovation work and referrals from contractors. Here is the kind of brief that would give a designer enough to work with.

Sample small-business website brief
Brief itemWhat to decideElectrician example
Primary customer actionThe one outcome the site should make easiestRequest a service call or estimate by phone or form
Service hierarchyWhich work gets the strongest pages and calls to actionEmergency and service repair first, renovations second, light commercial third
AudienceWho the site is really forHomeowners who need help now, plus contractors looking for a reliable subtrade
Existing assetsWhat can be reusedLogo, truck photography, several before-and-after photos, licence and insurance details, current service list
Pages to keep or rebuildCurrent URLs and content worth preservingService pages, contact page and any local pages that still bring enquiries
IntegrationsSystems the website must connect withForm enquiries to email, call tracking if used, optional online estimate request
Editing ownerWho maintains the site after launchOffice manager updates photos, reviews and seasonal notices
Budget assumptionsWhat the owner expects to be includedDesign, build, basic copy cleanup, search foundations, launch support
Sign-offWho approves each stageOwner approves structure and design; office manager proofreads service details

The point is not that every electrician needs this exact site. The point is that the brief turns a vague desire for something more professional into decisions about priority, proof, content, ownership and scope.

sections.title: Send the brief, then ask better questions
sections.body:
Once the brief is written, send it to a small shortlist rather than every designer you can find. Then use the replies to test understanding. A good response will reflect your priorities back to you, ask about the missing pieces and explain what would change the price. A weak response will ignore the brief and sell a standard package.

If you are planning a 2027 website, this is a good time to get the brief down while the decisions are fresh. If you want a second set of eyes on the brief, the service hierarchy or the questions to ask before you sign, contact me and we can look at the project properly.

faqs: Should I write the brief before asking for quotes, or can the designer help create it?

Write a first version before asking for quotes. A designer can help refine it, but the owner still needs to decide the customer action, service priority, approval path and what content already exists.
How detailed should a small-business website brief be?

It should be detailed enough that two designers would understand the same project. That does not mean it has to be long. It means the scope, assets, integrations, editing owner and sign-off path are clear.
What if I do not know which website platform or CMS I need?

Say that in the brief. Describe how you expect to edit the site, what systems it needs to connect with and what kind of support you want. Then ask each designer to explain the platform they recommend and why.
What should I decide before asking a designer for an estimate?

Name the main customer action, the services that matter most, the pages needed and the content you can supply. List booking, payment or CRM connections and who will approve the work. Explain your budget and editing needs so the designer can recommend a scope instead of pricing an undefined idea.
What if different people in the business want different things from the website?

Choose an accountable project owner and agree how decisions will be made before design begins. Separate essential customer tasks from internal preferences, then rank requests against the business goal. Record unresolved questions in the brief so they can be priced or decided deliberately instead of appearing as late revisions.
